claim: Current in vitro models of developmental blood formation lack spatio-temporal accuracy and weakly replicate successive waves of hematopoiesis.
source: Current in vitro models of developmental blood formation lack spatio-temporal accuracy and weakly replicate successive waves of hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing models, presented as established knowledge in the field to motivate the study.

claim: The hemogenic gastruloid (haemGx) model captures multi-wave blood formation.
source: Herein, we describe a mouse embryonic stem cell (SC)-derived 3D hemogenic gastruloid (haemGx) that captures multi-wave blood formation, progenitor specification from hemogenic endothelium (HE), and generates hematopoietic progenitors capable of short-term engraftment of immunodeficient mice upon maturation in an in vivo niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including flow cytometry, scRNA-seq, and functional assays.

claim: The haemGx model generates hematopoietic progenitors capable of short-term engraftment of immunodeficient mice upon maturation in an in vivo niche.
source: Herein, we describe a mouse embryonic stem cell (SC)-derived 3D hemogenic gastruloid (haemGx) that captures multi-wave blood formation, progenitor specification from hemogenic endothelium (HE), and generates hematopoietic progenitors capable of short-term engraftment of immunodeficient mice upon maturation in an in vivo niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from adrenal gland implantation experiments showing BFP+ engraftment in bone marrow and spleen.

claim: MNX1-driven leukemia represents the commonest genetic abnormality unique to the infant group.
source: We focused on MNX1-driven leukemia, representing the commonest genetic abnormality unique to the infant group.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on infant AML, as referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: Enforced MNX1 expression in haemGx promotes the expansion and in vitro transformation of yolk sac-like erythroid-myeloid progenitors at the HE-to-hematopoietic transition.
source: Enforced MNX1 expression in haemGx promotes the expansion and in vitro transformation of yolk sac-like erythroid-myeloid progenitors at the HE-to-hematopoietic transition to faithfully recapitulate patient transcriptional signatures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including flow cytometry, serial replating assays, and RNA-seq analysis of MNX1-overexpressing haemGx.

claim: MNX1 overexpression in haemGx faithfully recapitulates patient transcriptional signatures.
source: Enforced MNX1 expression in haemGx promotes the expansion and in vitro transformation of yolk sac-like erythroid-myeloid progenitors at the HE-to-hematopoietic transition to faithfully recapitulate patient transcriptional signatures.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis showing enrichment of MNX1-r patient signatures in MNX1-overexpressing haemGx cells.

claim: The first wave of hematopoiesis produces unipotent red blood cell and macrophage precursors in the yolk sac (YS) from an angioblast precursor which can also form endothelium.
source: The first wave of hematopoiesis produces unipotent red blood cell and macrophage precursors in the yolk sac (YS) from an angioblast precursor which can also form endothelium; it occurs at mouse embryo day (E)7-E7.5 (Fujimoto et al., 2001; McGrath and Palis, 2005; Moore and Metcalf, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: The first wave of hematopoiesis occurs at mouse embryo day (E)7-E7.5.
source: The first wave of hematopoiesis produces unipotent red blood cell and macrophage precursors in the yolk sac (YS) from an angioblast precursor which can also form endothelium; it occurs at mouse embryo day (E)7-E7.5 (Fujimoto et al., 2001; McGrath and Palis, 2005; Moore and Metcalf, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: The definitive wave produces oligopotent erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) in the YS at E8-E8.5.
source: The subsequent wave, known as definitive, produces: first, oligopotent erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) in the YS (E8-E8.5); and later myelo-lymphoid progenitors (MLPs – E9.5-E10), multipotent progenitors (MPPs – E10-E11.5), and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs – E10.5-E11.5), in the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region of the embryo proper (Ivanovs et al., 2011; McGrath et al., 2015; Palis et al., 1999; Medvinsky and Dzierzak, 1996; Medvinsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: Myelo-lymphoid progenitors (MLPs) are produced at E9.5-E10 in the AGM region.
source: The subsequent wave, known as definitive, produces: first, oligopotent erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) in the YS (E8-E8.5); and later myelo-lymphoid progenitors (MLPs – E9.5-E10), multipotent progenitors (MPPs – E10-E11.5), and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs – E10.5-E11.5), in the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region of the embryo proper (Ivanovs et al., 2011; McGrath et al., 2015; Palis et al., 1999; Medvinsky and Dzierzak, 1996; Medvinsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: Multipotent progenitors (MPPs) are produced at E10-E11.5 in the AGM region.
source: The subsequent wave, known as definitive, produces: first, oligopotent erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) in the YS (E8-E8.5); and later myelo-lymphoid progenitors (MLPs – E9.5-E10), multipotent progenitors (MPPs – E10-E11.5), and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs – E10.5-E11.5), in the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region of the embryo proper (Ivanovs et al., 2011; McGrath et al., 2015; Palis et al., 1999; Medvinsky and Dzierzak, 1996; Medvinsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are produced at E10.5-E11.5 in the AGM region.
source: The subsequent wave, known as definitive, produces: first, oligopotent erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) in the YS (E8-E8.5); and later myelo-lymphoid progenitors (MLPs – E9.5-E10), multipotent progenitors (MPPs – E10-E11.5), and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs – E10.5-E11.5), in the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region of the embryo proper (Ivanovs et al., 2011; McGrath et al., 2015; Palis et al., 1999; Medvinsky and Dzierzak, 1996; Medvinsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: Definitive blood waves are characteristically specified from a specialized HE through a process of endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT).
source: Definitive blood waves are characteristically specified from a specialized HE through a process of endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT) (Zovein et al., 2008; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: HSC specification from HE is the last event in hematopoietic development and occurs in characteristic cell clusters found on the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta.
source: HSC specification from HE is the last event in hematopoietic development and occurs in characteristic cell clusters found on the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (Ivanovs et al., 2011; Boisset et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: All blood cell types enter circulation from their original locations and migrate to the fetal liver (FL).
source: All blood cell types enter circulation from their original locations and migrate to the fetal liver (FL) (Ciriza et al., 2013; Ghiaur et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: Most embryonic blood progenitors are transient and sustain blood production exclusively during embryonic development, through differentiation.
source: Most embryonic blood progenitors are transient and sustain blood production exclusively during embryonic development, through differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field of embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: HSCs make little or no contribution to embryonic and fetal blood; instead, they proliferate (i.e. self-renew) to expand their numbers.
source: In contrast, HSCs make little or no contribution to embryonic and fetal blood; instead, they proliferate (i.e. self-renew) to expand their numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field of embryonic hematopoiesis.

claim: At least a subset of HSCs migrates to the bone marrow (BM) niche at the end of gestation and balances self-renewal and differentiation to maintain blood production throughout the entire post-natal life.
source: At least a subset of HSCs migrates to the bone marrow (BM) niche at the end of gestation and balances self-renewal and differentiation to maintain blood production throughout the entire post-natal life (Bowie et al., 2006; Kikuchi and Kondo, 2006; Ganuza et al., 2022; Yokomizo et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on HSC biology.

claim: Leukemia is the most common malignancy and the most common cause of cancer-related death in the pediatric age group.
source: Leukemia is the most common malignancy and the most common cause of cancer-related death in the pediatric age group (Steliarova-Foucher et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on pediatric cancer epidemiology.

claim: Several pediatric leukemias originate in utero.
source: Several pediatric leukemias originate in utero, and a subset of these are driven by mutations exclusive to the pediatric group (Masetti et al., 2015; Cazzola et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on pediatric leukemia.

claim: A subset of pediatric leukemias are driven by mutations exclusive to the pediatric group.
source: Several pediatric leukemias originate in utero, and a subset of these are driven by mutations exclusive to the pediatric group (Masetti et al., 2015; Cazzola et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on pediatric leukemia.

claim: Pediatric-exclusive mutations target blood cell types restricted to development or depend on signals that are specific to embryonic hematopoietic niches.
source: Such pediatric-exclusive mutations target blood cell types restricted to development or depend on signals that are specific to embryonic hematopoietic niches, effectively defining distinct biological entities to adult malignancies (Cazzola et al., 2020; Bolouri et al., 2018; Chaudhury et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on pediatric leukemia.

claim: t(7;12) (q36;p13) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is driven by rearrangement and overexpression of the MNX1 gene locus.
source: One such example is t(7;12) (q36;p13) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) driven by rearrangement and overexpression of the MNX1 gene locus: MNX1-rearranged (MNX1-r) AML is restricted to infants under the age of 2 and carries a high risk of relapse and poor survival (Ragusa et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on MNX1-rearranged AML.

claim: MNX1-rearranged (MNX1-r) AML is restricted to infants under the age of 2.
source: One such example is t(7;12) (q36;p13) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) driven by rearrangement and overexpression of the MNX1 gene locus: MNX1-rearranged (MNX1-r) AML is restricted to infants under the age of 2 and carries a high risk of relapse and poor survival (Ragusa et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on MNX1-rearranged AML.

claim: MNX1-rearranged (MNX1-r) AML carries a high risk of relapse and poor survival.
source: One such example is t(7;12) (q36;p13) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) driven by rearrangement and overexpression of the MNX1 gene locus: MNX1-rearranged (MNX1-r) AML is restricted to infants under the age of 2 and carries a high risk of relapse and poor survival (Ragusa et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on MNX1-rearranged AML.

claim: MNX1 is a developmental gene required for specification of motor neurons and pancreatic acinar cells.
source: MNX1 is a developmental gene required for specification of motor neurons and pancreatic acinar cells (Thaler et al., 1999; Harrison et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on MNX1 function.

claim: MNX1 is not known to participate in embryonic hematopoiesis.
source: MNX1 is not known to participate in embryonic hematopoiesis; however, it has been discordantly described to be expressed in some subsets of adult hematopoietic cells (Deguchi and Kehrl, 1991; Nagel et al., 2005; Wildenhain et al., 2012; Taketani et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of evidence in the literature for MNX1 function in embryonic hematopoiesis, as indicated by the citations.

claim: MNX1 has been discordantly described to be expressed in some subsets of adult hematopoietic cells.
source: MNX1 is not known to participate in embryonic hematopoiesis; however, it has been discordantly described to be expressed in some subsets of adult hematopoietic cells (Deguchi and Kehrl, 1991; Nagel et al., 2005; Wildenhain et al., 2012; Taketani et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on MNX1 expression.

claim: MNX1 is ectopically expressed in AML cells carrying one of a variable set of t(7;12) translocations which place the normally silent MNX1 gene under the control of ETV6 regulatory elements.
source: It is ectopically expressed in AML cells carrying one of a variable set of t(7;12) translocations which place the normally silent MNX1 gene under the control of ETV6 regulatory elements (Weichenhan et al., 2023; Bousquets-Muñoz et al., 2024; Ragusa et al., 2023; Ballabio et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on MNX1-rearranged AML.

claim: ETV6 is required for hematopoietic cell specification from HE via VEGF signalling.
source: ETV6 is required for hematopoietic cell specification from HE via VEGF signalling (Ciau-Uitz et al., 2010), potentially positioning MNX1 within a critical embryonic hemogenic regulatory network.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on ETV6 function.

claim: Gastruloid models have emerged as robust avatars of early development, self-organizing processes of symmetry breaking, elongation, multi-axis formation, somitogenesis and early organogenesis, with remarkable similarity to embryo processes in space and time.
source: In the last few years, gastruloid models have emerged as robust avatars of early development, self-organizing processes of symmetry breaking, elongation, multi-axis formation, somitogenesis and early organogenesis, with remarkable similarity to embryo processes in space and time (van den Brink and van Oudenaarden, 2021; Beccari et al., 2018; van den Brink et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on gastruloid models.

claim: A variant gastruloid culture system was able to recapitulate YS blood formation with erythroid and myeloid cellularity.
source: Relevant to blood formation, a variant gastruloid culture system, which successfully organizes a heart primordium (Rossi et al., 2021), was also able to recapitulate YS blood formation with erythroid and myeloid cellularity (Rossi et al., 2021; Rossi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on gastruloid models of hematopoiesis.

claim: The haemGx protocol includes an indispensable pulse of Activin A to induce hemato-endothelial programmes via TGF-β signalling.
source: The haemGx protocol includes an indispensable pulse of Activin A to induce hemato-endothelial programmes via TGF-β signalling (visible by proxy of GFP-tagged Flk1 activation), in addition to the characteristic gastruloid patterning via WNT activation by CHI99021 supplementation at 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Activin A is required for Flk1-GFP activation and subsequent hematopoietic development.

claim: Hemato-endothelial programs were promoted through addition of VEGF and FGF2 at 72 hr.
source: We promoted hemato-endothelial programs through addition of VEGF and FGF2 at 72 hr (Sroczynska et al., 2009; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior literature on hematopoietic differentiation.

claim: A polarized Flk1-GFP-expressing branched endothelial network was observed in haemGx.
source: We observed extension of a polarized Flk1-GFP-expressing branched endothelial network (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing Flk1-GFP expression in haemGx.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis revealed the onset of VE-cadherin+ C-Kit+ cells suggestive of EHT, with a peak at 120–144 hr.
source: Flow cytometry analysis revealed the onset of VE-cadherin+ C-Kit+ cells suggestive of EHT, with a peak at 120–144 hr (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing the time-dependent appearance of VE-cadherin+ C-Kit+ cells.

claim: A surge in CD41+ candidate hematopoietic cells was observed at 144 hr in haemGx.
source: This was followed by a surge in CD41+ candidate hematopoietic cells at 144 hr (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing the time-dependent appearance of CD41+ cells.

claim: A 24 hr pulse of sonic hedgehog (Shh) between 144–168 hr was incorporated to mimic the aortic patterning that precedes cluster formation.
source: We incorporated a 24 hr pulse of sonic hedgehog (Shh) between 144–168 hr to mimic the aortic patterning that precedes cluster formation (Figure 1A; Rybtsov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental design and citation to prior literature on HSC development.

claim: Continued exposure to VEGF after the Shh pulse resulted in specification of CD45+ hematopoietic cells progenitors.
source: Continued exposure to VEGF after the Shh pulse resulted in specification of CD45+ hematopoietic cells progenitors (Figure 1C–E), which were apparent after 168 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing the time-dependent appearance of CD45+ cells.

claim: The proportion of CD45+ cells was enhanced by the addition of SCF, FLT3L, and TPO.
source: The proportion of CD45+ cells was enhanced by the addition of SCF, FLT3L, and TPO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), a combination of cytokines routinely used for HSC maintenance; conversely, it did not require continued addition of FGF2 after 168 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), which was omitted.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing CD45+ cell frequencies with and without SCF, FLT3L, and TPO.

claim: CD45+ cells were present in a small number of 'cluster'-like structures adjacent to Flk1-GFP+ Kit+ endothelium.
source: CD45+ cells, some of which co-expressed C-Kit, were present in a small number of 'cluster'-like structures adjacent to Flk1-GFP+ Kit+ endothelium (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data showing the spatial organization of CD45+ cells.

claim: Time-dependent specification of C-Kit+, CD41+, and CD45+ cells in haemGx could be obtained with other mouse ES cell lines, including commonly used E14Tg2a (E14) cells.
source: Time-dependent specification of C-Kit+, CD41+, and CD45+ cells in haemGx could be obtained with other mouse ES cell lines, including commonly used E14Tg2a (E14) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-H), with successful specification of comparable frequencies of CD45+ progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), attesting to the reproducibility of the protocol across cell lines of different genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data from haemGx generated from different ES cell lines.

claim: Endothelial identity of Flk1-GFP+ populations was detectable by flow cytometry through the presence of endothelial markers CD31 and CD34.
source: Endothelial identity of Flk1-GFP+ populations was also detectable by flow cytometry through the presence of endothelial markers CD31 and CD34 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing co-expression of Flk1-GFP with CD31 and CD34.

claim: Subsets of CD41+ and CD45+ hematopoietic cells co-express CD31 and CD34.
source: Given the co-expression of CD31 and CD34 with hematopoietic progenitors emerging from HE, we inspected CD41+ and CD45+ cells for the presence of these markers. Indeed, we found that subsets of CD41+ and CD45+ hematopoietic cells co-express CD31 and CD34 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), with increased relative representation of hemato-endothelial markers within CD41+ cells at 144 hr and CD45+ at 216 hr (Figure 2C), consistent with two successive waves of hemogenic emergence from HE.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing co-expression of hemato-endothelial markers.

claim: CD45+ cells from 216 hr haemGx co-expressed C-Kit, Flk1-GFP, and VE-cadherin, a phenotype enriched in emergent hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) in the AGM.
source: CD45+ cells from 216 hr haemGx also co-expressed C-Kit, Flk1-GFP, and VE-cadherin, a phenotype enriched in emergent hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) in the AGM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data and citation to prior literature on HSPC phenotypes.

claim: The phenotype CD45+ C-Kit+ Flk1-GFP+ VE-cadherin+ is detected in 1.8% of CD45+ cells on average, corresponding to an estimated 8 cells per haemGx.
source: The phenotype is detected in 1.8% of CD45+ cells on average (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), corresponding to an estimated 8 cells per haemGx.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data quantifying the frequency of this phenotype.

claim: Analysis of the haemGx progenitor content at 216 hr using multipotential CFC assays revealed the presence of >50 CFC/haemGx, of which an average of seven have mixed-lineage granulocytic-monocytic-erythroid (GEM) potential.
source: In agreement, analysis of the haemGx progenitor content at 216 hr using multipotential CFC assays (Figure 2D–E) revealed the presence of >50 CFC/haemGx, of which an average of seven have mixed-lineage granulocytic-monocytic-erythroid (GEM) potential, numerically matching the estimated number of HSPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by CFC assay data quantifying colony-forming potential.

claim: Other progenitors in haemGx were predominantly granulo-monocytic (GM) and erythroid (E) progenitors.
source: Other progenitors were predominantly granulo-monocytic (GM) and erythroid (E) progenitors (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by CFC assay data showing the types of colonies formed.

claim: Analysis of the cellularity of dissociated haemGx at the 216 hr timepoint using Giemsa-Wright stained cytospins revealed differentiated cells of G, M, E, and megakaryocytic lineages.
source: Analysis of the cellularity of dissociated haemGx at the 216 hr timepoint using Giemsa-Wright stained cytospins revealed differentiated cells of G, M, E, and megakaryocytic lineages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), putatively reflecting the progeny of EMP-like cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytospin analysis showing differentiated cell morphologies.

claim: Temporal progression of expression of key markers was observed by qPCR, configuring a sustained hemato-endothelial program from 120 hr through 216 hr.
source: We observed temporal progression of expression of key markers by real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR), configuring a sustained hemato-endothelial program from 120 hr through 216 hr (Dll4 and Mecom), and the generation of hematopoietic populations based on the time-dependent patterns of Myb, Runx1, Hlf, and Hoxa9 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing time-dependent gene expression patterns.

claim: Myb peaks at 144 hr, coincident with the emergence of CD41+ cells, which are postulated to have YS-like EMP characteristics.
source: We note that Myb peaks at 144 hr, coincident with the emergence of CD41+ cells, which we postulate to have YS-like EMP characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing Myb expression and inference from the timing of CD41+ cell emergence.

claim: Runx1 has a bimodal pattern peaking at 144 hr, and later at 216 hr, suggesting the presence of two distinct hematopoietic waves.
source: On the other hand, Runx1 has a bimodal pattern peaking at 144 hr, and later at 216 hr, suggesting the presence of two distinct hematopoietic waves.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing Runx1 expression and inference from the bimodal pattern.

claim: The later timepoint of 216 hr has significantly higher expression of both Hoxa9 and Hlf raising the possibility that the second wave corresponds to the specification of AGM-like HSPC.
source: The later timepoint of 216 hr has significantly higher expression of both Hoxa9 and Hlf raising the possibility that the second wave indeed corresponds to the specification of AGM-like HSPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing Hoxa9 and Hlf expression and inference from their association with AGM hematopoiesis.

claim: Upon EZH2 inhibition via treatment with GSK216 from 120 hr onwards, a reduction of CD41+ cells was observed selectively at 144 hr, with no change in CD45+ cells at the later timepoint of 216 hr.
source: Upon EZH2 inhibition via treatment with GSK216 from 120 hr onwards, we observed a reduction of CD41+ cells selectively at 144 hr, with no change in CD45+ cells at the later timepoint of 216 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing CD41+ and CD45+ cell frequencies with and without EZH2 inhibitor.

claim: The vulnerability of 144 hr CD41+ to EZH2 inhibition suggests that they include YS-like EMP and do not predominantly reflect EZH2-independent primitive YS hematopoiesis.
source: This suggests that the cells present at the later timepoint may not be the progeny of the former, thus supporting recapitulation of two independent hematopoietic waves, the latter putatively AGM. Additionally, the vulnerability of 144 hr CD41+ to EZH2 inhibition suggests that they include YS-like EMP and do not predominantly reflect EZH2-independent primitive YS hematopoiesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the EZH2 inhibition data and citation to prior literature on EZH2 function in hematopoiesis.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing time-course analysis of haemGx cell specification was performed, profiling a total of 846 cells using the Smart-Seq2 protocol.
source: We sorted cells from two independent haemGx cultures at 120, 144, 168, 192, and 216 hr, and profiled a total of 846 cells using the Smart-Seq2 protocol (Picelli et al., 2014; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the scRNA-seq experimental design and citation to the Smart-Seq2 protocol.

claim: Library preparation and sequencing generated an average of 120,000 reads/cell, which were mapped to an average of 4000 genes/cell.
source: Library preparation and sequencing generated an average of 120,000 reads/cell, which were mapped to an average of 4000 genes/cell, with minimal signs of cell stress/death as measured by mitochondrial DNA fraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quality control metrics from the scRNA-seq data.

claim: 12 cell clusters were identified in the scRNA-seq analysis, of which 2 (clusters 0 and 5) almost exactly mapped to C-Kit+ cells, 2 (clusters 1 and 8) contained CD45+ sorted cells, and cluster 4 uniquely captured the CD41+ cells observed at 144 hr.
source: We identified 12 cell clusters of which 2 (clusters 0 and 5) almost exactly mapped to C-Kit+ cells (also positive for Sca-1), 2 (clusters 1 and 8) contained CD45+ sorted cells, and cluster 4 uniquely captured the CD41+ cells observed at 144 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq clustering analysis and mapping to sorted cell populations.

claim: Top classifier genes for clusters 0 and 5 had endothelial affiliation.
source: Top classifier genes for clusters 0 and 5 had endothelial affiliation (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2), and the cellular composition of the clusters broadly reflected their time signature (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D): cluster 5 comprised 144 hr cells and cluster 0 included most C-Kit+ cells at 192 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster 5 occupied the vicinity of 144 hr CD41+ cells, which carried an erythroid-biased signature.
source: Cluster 5 occupied the vicinity of 144 hr CD41+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which carried an erythroid-biased signature (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq clustering analysis and gene expression signatures.

claim: 192/216h-CD45+ cells in cluster 8 expressed myeloid and lymphoid genes.
source: On the other hand, 192/216h-CD45+ cells in cluster 8 expressed myeloid and lymphoid genes (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Clusters of cells present at later timepoints matched mesenchymal stromal cell and autonomic neuron signatures, potentially configuring incipient formation of niches relevant to production of HSCs.
source: The remaining clusters largely corresponded to time-restricted unfractionated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, bottom panel), with clusters of cells present at later timepoints matching mesenchymal stromal cell and autonomic neuron signatures (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), potentially configuring incipient formation of niches relevant to production of HSCs (Kapeni et al., 2022; Fitch et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell type enrichment analysis of scRNA-seq data and citation to prior literature on HSC niches.

claim: Pecam, Cd34, and Mecom expression coincided with clusters 0 and 3, which capture C-Kit+ cells at 144 and 192 hr, respectively.
source: We observed a coincidence of Pecam, Cd34, and Mecom expression with clusters 0 and 3, which capture C-Kit+ cells at 144 and 192 hr, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: CD41+ and CD45+-sorted clusters show expression of Runx1, confirming their hematopoietic affiliation.
source: CD41+ and CD45+-sorted clusters, on the other hand, show expression of Runx1, confirming their hematopoietic affiliation.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: Cd44 is detected predominantly in C-Kit+-enriched cluster 3 and CD45+-sorted clusters 1 and 4, corresponding to the later timepoints of 192 and 216 hr.
source: Cd44, which is upregulated at the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT) and in association with the AGM region (Oatley et al., 2020; Fadlullah et al., 2022), is detected predominantly in C-Kit+-enriched cluster 3 and CD45+-sorted clusters 1 and 4, corresponding to the later timepoints of 192 and 216 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis and citation to prior literature on Cd44 function.

claim: Significant increases in expression of VE-cadherin (Cdh5), Sox17, as well as Cd34, Cd44, and Procr were observed in 192 hr, endothelial-enriched, C-Kit+ cells.
source: This supports the notion that the later timepoints may capture AGM-like EHT, which is also suggested by significant increases in expression of VE-cadherin (Cdh5), Sox17, as well as Cd34, Cd44, and Procr (Fadlullah et al., 2022; Frankish et al., 2019; Oatley et al., 2020) in 192 hr, endothelial-enriched, C-Kit+ cells (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis and citation to prior literature on AGM markers.

claim: 192 hr C-Kit+ cells express arterial endothelial markers, including Flt1, Efnb2, and Dll4 steadily at both timepoints.
source: Important in this context, these cells express arterial endothelial markers, including Flt1, Efnb2, and Dll4 steadily at both timepoints (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: Hoxa9 expression is detected exclusively in C-Kit and CD45-sorted cells in the 192 and 216 hr-timepoints of haemGx differentiation.
source: Hoxa9 expression also associates with arterial specification and definitive AGM-like hematopoiesis: albeit at low frequency, it is detected exclusively in C-Kit and CD45-sorted cells in the 192 and 216 hr-timepoints of haemGx differentiation (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: Cells expressing Hoxa9 also express Mllt3 and, rarely, Hlf, compatible with incipient specification of an AGM-like definitive blood program.
source: These cells also express Mllt3 and, rarely, Hlf, compatible with incipient specification of an AGM-like definitive blood program (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis and inference from the association of these genes with AGM hematopoiesis.

claim: Mllt3 is additionally expressed in CD41+-sorted cells of cluster 2, in line with its role in early erythroid and megakaryocytic lineage identity.
source: Mllt3 is additionally expressed in CD41+-sorted cells of cluster 2, in line with its role in early erythroid and megakaryocytic lineage identity (Pina et al., 2008); Myb is also more frequently expressed in this population (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis and citation to prior literature on Mllt3 function.

claim: Ikzf1 gradually increases its expression, and indeed frequency, in 216 hr-CD45+ sorted cells.
source: In contrast, Ikzf1, which regulates lymphoid specification (Huang et al., 2019), gradually increases its expression, and indeed frequency, in 216 hr-CD45+ sorted cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis and citation to prior literature on Ikzf1 function.

claim: A handover from erythroid/megakaryocytic to myelo-lymphoid lineage affiliation is apparent between 144 hr and 216 hr haemGx blood cells.
source: A handover from erythroid/megakaryocytic to myelo-lymphoid lineage affiliation is apparent between 144 hr and 216 hr haemGx blood cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis showing changes in lineage-affiliated gene expression.

claim: A small number of erythroid-affiliated cells at 216 hr express adult globins, suggesting a definitive origin.
source: Of note, a small number of erythroid-affiliated cells at 216 hr express adult globins, suggesting a definitive origin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression analysis and inference from the expression of adult globins.

claim: Projections of haemGx scRNA-seq data onto Hou et al., 2020 positioned clusters 0 and 3, corresponding to endothelium, including arterial endothelium and HE-like cells, between days E8.5 and E10.
source: Projections onto Hou et al., 2020 positioned clusters 0 and 3, corresponding to endothelium, including arterial endothelium and HE-like cells, between days E8.5 and E10, putatively spanning YS-like and AGM-like blood formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by projection analysis of scRNA-seq data onto published embryonic datasets.

claim: A subset of CD45+-sorted cells, as well as a small numbers of CD41+ cells from cluster 2 projected onto E10 HE and intra-aortic cluster (IAC) cells, suggesting the presence of definitive HSPC or their precursors in haemGx.
source: A subset of CD45+-sorted cells, as well as a small numbers of CD41+ cells from cluster 2 projected onto E10 HE and intra-aortic cluster (IAC) cells, suggesting the presence of definitive HSPC or their precursors in haemGx (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by projection analysis of scRNA-seq data onto published embryonic datasets.

claim: A large proportion of CD41+-sorted cells matched the identity of YS EMP when projected onto Zhu et al., 2020.
source: We matched the identity of a large proportion of CD41+-sorted cells to YS EMP, with some of the same cluster 2 cells mapping to erythroid progenitors, and some later CD45+-sorted cells resembling myeloid progenitors (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by projection analysis of scRNA-seq data onto published embryonic datasets.

claim: A subset of CD45+-sorted cells mapped to IAC and lymphoid-myeloid primed progenitors (LMPP) in the FL when projected onto Zhu et al., 2020.
source: On the other hand, a subset of CD45+-sorted cells mapped to IAC and lymphoid-myeloid primed progenitors (LMPP) in the FL (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3), compatible with the presence of AGM-like definitive HSPC in haemGx.
evidence: This claim is supported by projection analysis of scRNA-seq data onto published embryonic datasets.

claim: Some CD41+-sorted cells also map to IAC, and indeed to HE, suggesting that this earlier population may contain HSPC precursors, in addition to YS-like progenitors.
source: Interestingly, some CD41+-sorted cells also map to IAC, and indeed to HE, suggesting that this earlier population may contain HSPC precursors, in addition to YS-like progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by projection analysis of scRNA-seq data onto published embryonic datasets and inference from the mapping results.

claim: Projection onto Thambyrajah et al., 2024 conflates YS-like and AGM-like progenitors onto the candidate HSC-enriched embryo AGM cluster 2.
source: Projection onto Thambyrajah et al., 2024 (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3), conflates YS-like and AGM-like progenitors onto the candidate HSC-enriched embryo AGM cluster 2, highlighting the similarity between transcriptional programs at different sites of embryonic blood emergence.
evidence: This claim is supported by projection analysis of scRNA-seq data onto published embryonic datasets.

claim: Transplantation of dissociated haemGx cells obtained at 192 and 216 hr into irradiated immunocompetent C57Bl/6 recipients, sub-lethally irradiated immunodeficient NSG mice, or non-conditioned NSGW41 hosts failed to detect signs of engraftment.
source: In early experiments, we had transplanted dissociated haemGx cells obtained at 192 and 216 hr into irradiated immunocompetent C57Bl/6 recipients, sub-lethally irradiated immunodeficient NSG mice, or non-conditioned NSGW41 hosts, but failed to detect signs of engraftment of peripheral blood, spleen (Spl) or bone marrow (BM) at 12 days (including absence of spleen colony formation), at 4–6 weeks (short-term engraftment), or beyond 8–10 weeks (long-term engraftment) by either flow cytometry detection of CD45.2 or by genomic DNA (gDNA) PCR analysis of the Flk1-GFP locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transplantation experiments.

claim: Implantation of undissociated haemGx in the adrenal gland of Nude mice was tested to support further 3D maturation in vivo.
source: We thus tested implantation of undissociated haemGx in the adrenal gland of Nude mice (Figure 4B), a topography more commonly used to support tumor development, but that was recently shown to be able to support HSC development, possibly with contributions from the sympathetic adrenal medullary niche (Schyrr et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental design and citation to prior literature on adrenal gland as a niche for HSC development.

claim: PCR analysis of BFP engraftment of the Spl and BM 4 weeks after adrenal implantation of 3 haemGx / animal detected BFP amplicon in both tissues in 3 of the 5 samples.
source: PCR analysis of BFP engraftment of the Spl and BM 4 weeks after adrenal implantation of 3 haemGx / animal detected BFP amplicon in both tissues in 3 of the 5 samples (#11, 12, and 15) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data showing BFP amplicon detection in recipient tissues.

claim: The same three animals showed BFP detection by flow cytometry above control, but no higher than 0.1%.
source: The same three animals showed BFP detection by flow cytometry above control, but no higher than 0.1% (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing BFP+ cell frequencies in recipient tissues.

claim: PCR engraftment was detectable in both erythroid Ter119+ and lympho-myeloid CD45+ fractions of the recipient animals.
source: PCR engraftment was nevertheless detectable in both erythroid Ter119+ and lympho-myeloid CD45+ fractions of the recipient animals showed PCR engraftment in both lineage fractions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data showing BFP amplicon detection in sorted lineage fractions.

claim: Analysis of engraftment 8 weeks after implantation showed low-level detection (<0.1%) of BFP+ cells with positivity for CD11b+ myeloid and B220+ lymphoid compartments in BM of 1 recipient.
source: Analysis of engraftment 8 weeks after implantation showed low-level detection (<0.1%) of BFP+ cells with positivity for CD11b+ myeloid and B220+ lymphoid compartments in BM of 1 recipient (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F-G); a fourth recipient had to be sacrificed early due to infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing BFP+ cell frequencies and lineage markers in recipient tissues.

claim: In some recipients, hematopoietic engraftment was accompanied by in situ growth and multi-tissue differentiation of the implanted haemGx.
source: Overall, implantation in the adrenal niche and/or preservation of the 3D architecture enabled low-level in vivo hematopoietic activity, although the mechanism remains unclear. In some recipients, hematopoietic engraftment was accompanied by in situ growth and multi-tissue differentiation of the implanted haemGx (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of implanted adrenal glands.

claim: Adrenal enlargement was not observed in all animals with hematopoietic engraftment, making it unlikely that hematopoietic activity results from teratoma formation by residual pluripotent cells.
source: However, adrenal enlargement was not observed in all animals with hematopoietic engraftment (e.g. 4 weeks' #11 had a normally sized adrenal, as did all animals analysed at 8 weeks), making it unlikely that hematopoietic activity results from teratoma formation by residual pluripotent cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the observation that not all engrafted animals showed adrenal enlargement.

claim: Late-stage haemGx (216 hr) may contain hematopoietic progenitors with some short-term engraftment potential but incomplete functional maturation, which are present at low frequency.
source: Late-stage haemGx (216 hr) may thus contain hematopoietic progenitors with some short-term engraftment potential but incomplete functional maturation, which are present at low frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the engraftment data showing low-level, short-term engraftment.

claim: Engraftment is erythro-myeloid at 4 weeks and lympho-myeloid at 8 weeks, reflecting different classes of progenitors, putatively of YS-like and AGM-like affiliation.
source: Engraftment is erythro-myeloid at 4 weeks and lympho-myeloid at 8 weeks, reflecting different classes of progenitors, putatively of YS-like and AGM-like affiliation.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the lineage analysis of engrafted cells at different timepoints.

claim: Forms of AML unique to the first 2 years of life – infant (inf)AML – have been shown to transform fetal liver (FL) but not adult hematopoietic cells.
source: In particular, forms of AML unique to the first 2 years of life – infant (inf)AML – have been shown to transform fetal liver (FL) but not adult hematopoietic cells (Waraky et al., 2024; Mercher et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2011; Ragusa et al., 2023), compatible with targeting of a transient embryonic cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on infant AML.

claim: Analysis of MNX1-r patient transcriptional signatures for over-representation of cell atlas-defined affiliations indicates enrichment in cardiomyogenic, endothelial, HSC/progenitor, and mast cells.
source: In the case of t(7;12) AML (herein MNX1-r) (Ragusa et al., 2023), in which the translocation results in transformation-driving ectopic expression of MNX1 (Waraky et al., 2024), analysis of patient transcriptional signatures (Ragusa et al., 2022) for over-representation of cell atlas-defined affiliations, indicates enrichment in cardiomyogenic, endothelial, HSC/progenitor, and mast cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of patient transcriptomes.

claim: MNX1-OE haemGx activated polarized Flk1-GFP expression and elongated with similar kinetics to empty-vector (EV) control, albeit with formation of larger haemGx.
source: MNX1-OE haemGx activated polarized Flk1-GFP expression and elongated with similar kinetics to empty-vector (EV) control (Figure 5C), albeit with formation of larger haemGx (Figure 5D) denoting increased cellularity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and size quantification data comparing MNX1-OE and EV haemGx.

claim: From 192 hr onwards, MNX1-OE haemGx had a higher frequency of spontaneously contractile structures.
source: From 192 hr onwards, MNX1-OE haemGx had a higher frequency of spontaneously contractile structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), compatible with the cardiogenic cell association of patients' transcriptomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of contractile structures in MNX1-OE haemGx.

claim: A small but significant expansion of the C-Kit+ compartment was observed specifically at 144 hr in MNX1-OE haemGx.
source: We observed a small but significant expansion of the C-Kit+ compartment specifically at 144 hr (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing C-Kit+ cell frequencies in MNX1-OE and EV haemGx.

claim: DEGs between MNX1-OE and EV configured distinct MNX1-driven programs at 144 hr and 216 hr, with >80% genes timepoint-specific.
source: DEGs between MNX1-OE and EV (Supplementary file 4) configured distinct MNX1-driven programs at 144 hr and 216 hr, with >80% genes timepoint-specific (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis comparing MNX1-OE and EV haemGx at different timepoints.

claim: Both programs include up-regulation of hematopoietic-associated genes, capturing EHT and progenitor regulators at the earlier timepoint, and more differentiated effectors at 216 hr.
source: Both programs include up-regulation of hematopoietic-associated genes, capturing EHT and progenitor regulators (e.g. Runx1, and Epor and Zfpm1, respectively) at the earlier timepoint, and more differentiated effectors, e.g., Hba-a1, Hbb-bh1, and Il3ra at 216 hr, compatible with selective targeting and/or expansion of YS EMP-like cells and their later differentiated progeny (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis showing differential gene expression in MNX1-OE haemGx.

claim: An overview of transcriptional regulatory programs at both timepoints denotes a clearer hemogenic enrichment at 144 hr, with over-representation of GATA2, GATA1r and RUNX1 binding targets.
source: An overview of transcriptional regulatory programs at both timepoints denotes a clearer hemogenic enrichment at 144 hr, with over-representation of GATA2, GATA1r and RUNX1 binding targets (Figure 5I), putatively capturing an expansion of a HE-to-EMP-like transition, also represented in enriched GO categories related to VEGF signalling and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor binding site enrichment analysis and GO term enrichment analysis of DEGs.

claim: No enrichment of hemogenic transcription factor (TF)-ChIP targets or related gene ontologies (GO) categories was observed in MNX1-OE haemGx at 216 hr.
source: In contrast, no enrichment of hemogenic transcription factor (TF)-ChIP targets or related gene ontologies (GO) categories was observed in MNX1-OE haemGx at 216 hr (Figure 5I–J), suggesting specific targeting of YS-like hemogenic programs.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor binding site enrichment analysis and GO term enrichment analysis of DEGs.

claim: There was an enrichment in cardiogenic GO at 216 hr in MNX1-OE haemGx.
source: Instead, there was an enrichment in cardiogenic GO at 216 hr (Figure 5J), reflecting the increase in contractile foci in MNX1-OE late haemGx.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis of DEGs.

claim: MNX1-OE transcriptomes showed enrichment of haemGx HE cluster 5 and 0 signatures.
source: In support of an association with hemato-endothelial specification, MNX1-OE transcriptomes showed enrichment of haemGx HE cluster 5 and 0 signatures; the YS-EMP-like cluster 4 was also enriched (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of MNX1-OE transcriptomes against haemGx cluster signatures.

claim: Clusters 5 and 0 HE signatures were also enriched in MNX1-r infAML patient signatures.
source: Significantly, clusters 5 and 0 HE signatures were also enriched in MNX1-r infAML patient signatures (Ragusa et al., 2022; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C), putatively aligning MNX1-OE effects with HE and the hemogenic transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of patient transcriptomes against haemGx cluster signatures.

claim: Both 144 hr and 216 hr MNX1-OE haemGx replated for at least five platings and were significantly different to control (EV).
source: Both 144 hr (Figure 6A–B) and 216 hr (Figure 6C–D) MNX1-OE haemGx replated for at least five platings were significantly different to control (EV) (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial replating assay data comparing MNX1-OE and EV haemGx.

claim: Cells selected through replating were C-Kit+.
source: We analyzed early-stage (plate 1) and late-stage (plate 5) colonies by flow cytometry to identify the nature of the replating cells. Cells selected through replating were C-Kit+ (Figure 6E), matching the cell phenotype transiently enriched at 144 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of serially replated cells.

claim: MNX1-OE C-Kit+ cells co-expressed CD31.
source: MNX1-OE C-Kit+ cells co-expressed CD31 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), underpinning the endothelial signatures of MNX1-r leukemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of serially replated cells.

claim: Early replating of MNX1-OE haemGx also enriched for erythroid-affiliated Ter119+ cells, particularly when initiated from the 144 hr timepoint.
source: Early replating of MNX1-OE haemGx also enriched for erythroid-affiliated Ter119+ cells, particularly when initiated from the 144 hr timepoint (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), but this was not sustained through replating.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of serially replated cells.

claim: HsMNX1 reads were increased in MNX1-OE CFC samples, supporting selective expansion of transduced cells.
source: HsMNX1 reads were increased in MNX1-OE CFC samples, supporting selective expansion of transduced cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of serially replated cells.

claim: Cluster k14 had significant enrichment of MNX1-r signatures against all other AML subtypes.
source: Cluster k14 had significant enrichment of MNX1-r signatures against all other AML subtypes (Figure 7C), with considerable overlap between leading-edge (i.e. significantly-enriched) genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of k14 cluster genes against patient transcriptomes.

claim: k14 captures the subgroup of DEGs up-regulated upon CFC replating which are also up-regulated in MNX1-OE haemGx at 144 hr.
source: Importantly, k14 captures the subgroup of DEGs up-regulated upon CFC replating which are also up-regulated in MNX1-OE haemGx at 144 hr (Figure 7B), matching the time-dependent enrichment of the putative MNX1-OE propagating population.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of DEGs from RNA-seq data.

claim: Interrogation of cell-type-specific signatures within the k14 MNX1-r leading-edge genes against the single-cell PanglaoDB atlas captured similarities to hemogenic and non-hemogenic cell types, including interneuron, and other neural signatures.
source: Interrogation of cell-type-specific signatures within the k14 MNX1-r leading-edge genes against the single-cell PanglaoDB atlas captured similarities to hemogenic and non-hemogenic cell types, including interneuron, and other neural signatures (Figure 7D), which reflect MNX1 biological functions (Harrison et al., 1999; Thaler et al., 1999; Ragusa et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell type enrichment analysis of k14 leading-edge genes.

claim: The most highly significant signatures capture early developmental hemogenic components, such as 'endothelial cells' and 'erythroid cell precursors,' reflecting the 144 hr, putative YS affiliation of MNX1-OE haemGx.
source: The most highly significant signatures capture early developmental hemogenic components, such as 'endothelial cells' and 'erythroid cell precursors,' reflecting the 144 hr, putative YS affiliation of MNX1-OE haemGx.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell type enrichment analysis of k14 leading-edge genes and inference from the timing of MNX1-OE effects.

claim: The 'mast cells' affiliation of MNX1-r AML signatures within the haemGx k14 cluster is likely to reflect a YS EMP-like affiliation.
source: The 'mast cells' affiliation of MNX1-r AML signatures within the haemGx k14 cluster is also likely to reflect a YS EMP-like affiliation (Chia et al., 2023), and is accordingly aligned with MNX1-OE haemGx isolated at 144 hr (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell type enrichment analysis and citation to prior literature on mast cell development.

claim: Giemsa-Wright-stained cytospins of serially replated CFC assays initiated with 144 hr MNX1-OE cells showed a shift from blast-like at plate 3 to precursor cell morphology with some differentiated mast cells at plate 5.
source: Giemsa-Wright-stained cytospins of serially replated CFC assays initiated with 144 hr MNX1-OE cells showed a shift from blast-like at plate 3 to precursor cell morphology with some differentiated mast cells at plate 5 (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytospin analysis of serially replated cells.

claim: Mast cells were also observed in 216 hr-initiated colonies, but these were differentiated at an earlier plate, suggesting that MNX1-OE-responsive C-Kit+ progenitors experience maturation between 144 hr and 216 hr.
source: We also observed mast cells in 216 hr-initiated colonies (Figure 7E), but these were differentiated at an earlier plate, suggesting that MNX1-OE-responsive C-Kit+ progenitors experience maturation between 144 hr and 216 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytospin analysis of serially replated cells and inference from the timing of mast cell differentiation.
